name: Frontier AI labs
description: The labs training frontier models - OpenAI, Anthropic, Google DeepMind, Meta, xAI - whose scaling roadmaps define how much compute the world tries to buy.
whyItMatters: Every dollar of demand in this theme starts here: training-run ambitions set the order book for GPUs, packaging, memory, power and ultimately minerals.
risks: Model capability commoditises faster than pricing holds
Training capex outruns revenue and funding tightens
Regulation slows frontier-scale training runs

name: Hyperscale cloud platforms
description: The mega-cap cloud platforms - Microsoft, Amazon, Google, Meta, Oracle - converting AI demand into hundreds of billions of dollars of annual data-centre capex.
whyItMatters: Hyperscaler capex budgets are the single largest funding pipe in the theme; when they guide capex up or down, every supplier below them re-rates.
risks: Capex digestion phase after the initial buildout wave
Depreciation of short-lived GPU fleets pressures earnings
Antitrust and regulatory scrutiny of platform power

name: GPU neoclouds
description: Specialist GPU rental clouds - CoreWeave, Nebius, Crusoe, Lambda - that buy accelerators in bulk and lease capacity to labs and enterprises.
whyItMatters: Neoclouds are the marginal buyer of GPUs and the fastest signal of whether AI compute demand exceeds hyperscaler supply.
risks: GPU rental prices deflate as supply catches up
Heavy customer concentration in a few AI labs
Debt-financed fleets are fragile if utilisation slips

name: GPUs and AI accelerators
description: The chips that actually run training and inference - NVIDIA and AMD GPUs plus custom silicon like Google TPUs, Amazon Trainium and emerging ASICs.
whyItMatters: This is the theme's profit pool and its hardest constraint: accelerator supply, not ideas, has gated AI progress since 2023.
risks: Custom in-house silicon erodes the merchant GPU share
Export controls fence off major markets
A demand air pocket after multi-year over-ordering

name: Semiconductor capital equipment
description: The tools that make leading-edge chips possible - ASML lithography, Applied Materials, Lam Research and KLA deposition, etch and inspection systems.
whyItMatters: No new EUV-class tools, no new leading-edge capacity: equipment lead times of 12-24 months set the speed limit on how fast accelerator supply can grow.
risks: Export controls cap sales into China
Wafer-fab equipment spending is deeply cyclical
Single-source dependencies inside their own supply chains

name: Advanced packaging
description: CoWoS and similar 2.5D/3D packaging that bonds GPU dies to HBM stacks - dominated by TSMC with Amkor, ASE and Intel building capacity behind it.
whyItMatters: Packaging, not wafer starts, has repeatedly been the literal unit-volume cap on AI accelerator shipments since the boom began.
risks: Aggressive capacity adds eventually normalise the shortage
Heavy geographic concentration in Taiwan
Technology transitions like panel-level packaging reshuffle winners

name: HBM memory
description: High-bandwidth memory stacked next to the GPU die - an oligopoly of SK Hynix, Micron and Samsung whose output is sold out quarters in advance.
whyItMatters: Each accelerator generation needs more HBM per chip, so HBM supply and yield directly cap how many usable accelerators ship.
risks: Memory industry cyclicality returns once supply catches demand
Samsung qualification success adds a third full supplier
Yield missteps on next-generation stacks

name: Optical networking
description: The transceivers, switches and interconnect silicon - Broadcom, Coherent, Credo, Marvell - that lash tens of thousands of GPUs into one training cluster.
whyItMatters: Cluster scale is a networking problem: as clusters grow, optics content per GPU rises faster than GPU counts themselves.
risks: Architecture shifts like co-packaged optics strand incumbents
Steep per-unit price declines each product cycle
Chinese transceiver competition at the commodity end

name: Data centre REITs and operators
description: Owners and landlords of the buildings - Equinix, Digital Realty and private operators - leasing powered shells and colocation capacity to AI tenants.
whyItMatters: They control the scarcest real asset in the chain - land with secured grid connections - even though their economics are steadier than the silicon above them.
risks: Interest-rate sensitivity of REIT valuations
Hyperscalers self-build instead of leasing
Power availability delays new campus delivery

name: Power generation
description: The gas turbines, nuclear plants and renewables that feed AI campuses - from utility IPPs to behind-the-meter generation deals signed directly with hyperscalers.
whyItMatters: AI data centres are forecast to add power demand measured in tens of gigawatts; electrons have replaced chips as the long-pole constraint on new capacity.
risks: Gas turbine order books are sold out for years
Permitting and siting delays for new plants
Fuel price volatility passes through to economics

name: Grid transmission and interconnection
description: The high-voltage lines, substations and interconnection queues that connect new generation and new data centres to the grid.
whyItMatters: Interconnection queues of 3-7 years are now the slowest physical step in the entire AGI buildout - a campus without a grid connection is a warehouse.
risks: Permitting timelines measured in years not quarters
Regulated returns cap the upside of the buildout
Skilled transmission labour is itself scarce

name: Transformers and switchgear
description: Large power transformers, switchgear and electrical gear from Hitachi Energy, Siemens Energy, Eaton, GE Vernova and Schneider - the hardware every substation and data centre needs.
whyItMatters: Large transformer lead times stretched to 3-5 years; this is one of the most concrete, slowest-to-fix bottlenecks anywhere in the AI supply chain.
risks: Capacity expansions eventually normalise lead times
Grain-oriented electrical steel supply is itself constrained
Double-ordering in the backlog overstates real demand

name: Cooling and thermal management
description: Liquid cooling, cold plates, CDUs and thermal infrastructure - Vertiv, nVent and specialists - required as rack densities jump past 100kW.
whyItMatters: Next-generation accelerators cannot be air-cooled; liquid cooling adoption is mandatory, making thermal vendors a forced purchase per GPU rack.
risks: Technology shifts between cooling architectures
Crowding as industrials pile into the category
Direct dependence on the data-centre capex cycle

name: Nuclear and SMR for AI campuses
description: Restarted reactors, new nuclear PPAs and small modular reactor programs - Microsoft-Constellation, Amazon and Google SMR deals - aimed at firm clean power for AI.
whyItMatters: Nuclear is the only proven firm, carbon-free power source dense enough for gigawatt AI campuses, which is why hyperscalers are signing decades-long deals.
risks: Licensing timelines stretch deployments into the 2030s
First-of-a-kind SMR cost overruns
Public and political opposition to siting

name: Construction and engineering
description: The EPC firms, electrical contractors and skilled trades - Quanta, EMCOR, AECOM and peers - that physically build data centres, substations and power plants.
whyItMatters: Designs and chips mean nothing without electricians and ironworkers; skilled-labour capacity is the human bottleneck under every physical layer of the theme.
risks: Skilled electrical labour shortage limits delivery
Fixed-price contract overruns in a hot market
Backlog evaporates if the capex cycle turns

name: Critical minerals for AI hardware
description: The raw inputs at the bottom of the stack - copper for power, gallium for RF and power chips, rare earths for motors and silver for connectors.
whyItMatters: Every layer above ultimately resolves to mined material; export controls on gallium and structurally tight copper supply make this the deepest causal link in the chain.
risks: China export controls on gallium and rare earths
Commodity price volatility swamps equity returns
New mine supply takes a decade to arrive

name: Launch providers
description: The companies that put mass into orbit - SpaceX, Rocket Lab, ULA, Arianespace and emerging entrants - selling launch as the gateway service of the space economy.
whyItMatters: Launch cost per kilogram is the master variable of the entire theme; every downstream market expands or contracts with it.
risks: SpaceX's pricing umbrella caps everyone else's margins
A high-profile failure grounds a vehicle for months
Demand concentration in mega-constellation customers

name: Rocket engines
description: Engine developers and manufacturers - Raptor, BE-4, Archimedes, Aerojet Rocketdyne heritage engines - the highest-value and hardest subsystem of any launcher.
whyItMatters: Engine cadence and reusability determine launch cadence; an engine program slipping is the most common cause of a launcher slipping.
risks: Development cost overruns and test failures
Vertical integration by launch providers removes the merchant market
Long qualification cycles before revenue

name: Propellants and advanced materials
description: Methane, hydrogen and solid propellants plus the aerospace-grade alloys and composites that engines and airframes are built from.
whyItMatters: Reusable rockets turned propellant and materials into recurring operating inputs rather than one-off costs, tying launch economics to commodity supply.
risks: Commodity price exposure with thin pricing power
Aerospace qualification cycles slow new suppliers
Small standalone revenue pools for pure plays

name: Avionics and radiation-hardened electronics
description: Flight computers, guidance systems and rad-hard chips - BAE, Microchip, Teledyne and specialists - that survive launch loads and orbital radiation.
whyItMatters: Every vehicle and satellite needs qualified avionics, and the rad-hard supply base is narrow enough that a single supplier slip ripples across programs.
risks: Long qualification cycles delay design wins
ITAR and export controls shrink the addressable market
Commercial off-the-shelf parts undercut rad-hard pricing

name: Satellite manufacturers
description: Builders of satellite buses and constellations - from Airbus and Maxar to constellation factories like SpaceX's Starlink line and Rocket Lab's bus business.
whyItMatters: Satellites are the payload that justifies launch; constellation-scale manufacturing turned spacecraft from bespoke craft into a volume industry.
risks: Mega-constellation owners vertically integrate manufacturing
Per-satellite price deflation as volumes rise
Program delays cascade from component shortages

name: Communications and ground segment
description: Satellite broadband and connectivity operators plus the ground stations, terminals and antennas - Starlink, SES, Viasat, AST SpaceMobile, ground networks like KSAT.
whyItMatters: Connectivity is the largest commercial revenue pool in space today; the ground segment is the unglamorous toll booth every bit of data must pass through.
risks: Starlink price pressure on legacy operators
GEO satellite business in structural decline
Spectrum rights contention and regulation

name: Earth observation
description: Imaging and sensing constellations - Planet, BlackSky, ICEYE, Maxar - selling pictures, radar and analytics of the planet to governments and industry.
whyItMatters: EO is the proof case for space data as a recurring software-like revenue stream, and defence demand for persistent imaging keeps it funded.
risks: Imagery commoditises as supply of pixels explodes
Heavy dependence on government contracts
AI analytics value accrues to software layers above the constellations

name: Defence payloads
description: Military sensors, missile-warning payloads and secure comms hosted in orbit - the fastest-growing funded demand line in space, led by programs like the SDA's proliferated architecture.
whyItMatters: Defence budgets underwrite space demand independent of commercial cycles, and payload primes capture the highest-margin slice of each satellite.
risks: Program cancellations or restructuring
Classified work limits investor visibility
Budget cycles and continuing resolutions delay awards

name: In-space services
description: Orbital tugs, satellite servicing, refuelling and debris removal - Astroscale, Impulse Space, Northrop's MEV line - the logistics layer that emerges once orbit is busy.
whyItMatters: As constellations scale, moving, extending and disposing of spacecraft becomes a real cost line; this layer turns orbital congestion into a service market.
risks: Commercial demand is still largely unproven
Long development timelines before recurring revenue
Dependent on continued venture and government funding

name: Space insurance and logistics
description: Underwriters, brokers and supply-chain logistics that price launch and in-orbit risk and move flight hardware around the planet.
whyItMatters: Insurance is where the whole theme's risk gets priced in dollars; rising losses or shrinking capacity raise the cost of capital for every layer above.
risks: Large loss events shrink underwriting capacity
The premium pool is small relative to the industry it covers
Mega-constellations self-insure and bypass the market

name: Utilities and independent power producers
description: Regulated utilities and merchant IPPs - NextEra, Constellation, Vistra, Talen - that own generation and sell electrons into surging demand.
whyItMatters: They are the demand aggregators of the theme: data centres, electrification and reshoring all show up first as utility load growth and IPP power prices.
risks: Regulators cap allowed returns on the buildout
Rising interest rates pressure capital-heavy balance sheets
Fuel cost volatility in merchant markets

name: Transmission equipment
description: High-voltage transformers, cables, switchgear and HVDC systems - Hitachi Energy, Siemens Energy, Prysmian, Eaton - the hardware of grid expansion.
whyItMatters: Multi-year lead times on transformers and HV cable are the binding physical constraint on connecting new load and new generation anywhere in the West.
risks: Capacity expansion eventually works off the backlog
Raw material cost swings squeeze fixed-price orders
Execution risk on rapid factory expansions

name: Grid storage and batteries
description: Utility-scale battery systems and integrators - Tesla Energy, Fluence, Sungrow - that firm renewables and arbitrage peak power.
whyItMatters: Storage is what makes intermittent generation dispatchable; every gigawatt of solar and wind added pulls battery demand with it.
risks: Cell price deflation compresses integrator margins
Dominant Chinese supply chain invites tariff shocks
Policy and subsidy dependence in key markets

name: Grid engineering services
description: The contractors that design, build and maintain grid infrastructure - Quanta Services, MYR Group, MasTec - supplying the crews behind every upgrade.
whyItMatters: Transmission lines are built by linemen, not press releases; skilled-crew capacity converts utility capex plans into energised assets.
risks: The same labour scarcity that supports pricing limits growth
Fixed-price project execution risk
Utility capex cycles can pause large programs

name: Reactor and SMR developers
description: Builders of new nuclear capacity - Westinghouse AP1000s, GE Hitachi BWRX-300, NuScale, Oklo, TerraPower - plus restarts of shuttered plants.
whyItMatters: Reactors are the demand engine of the entire uranium chain; every announced SMR program and restart flows backward into fuel and enrichment demand.
risks: Licensing timelines stretch beyond investor patience
First-of-a-kind construction cost overruns
Pre-revenue developers carry heavy dilution risk

name: Uranium miners
description: Producers of mined uranium - Cameco, Kazatomprom, Paladin, NexGen and a long tail of developers - supplying the raw fuel for the reactor fleet.
whyItMatters: A decade of underinvestment left primary supply below reactor demand; restarts and new builds tighten a market with very slow supply response.
risks: Spot price volatility whipsaws sentiment
Idled capacity restarts faster than new demand lands
Geopolitical supply risk in Kazakhstan and Niger

name: Enrichment and fuel fabrication
description: Conversion, enrichment and fuel assembly - Urenco, Orano, Centrus and the push for Western HALEU capacity - turning mined uranium into reactor-ready fuel.
whyItMatters: Russia still controls roughly 40 percent of global enrichment; replacing it is the hardest, slowest and most strategic choke point in the nuclear revival.
risks: Transition risk as Russian supply bans phase in
HALEU demand depends on SMRs actually being built
Capex-heavy expansion with long payback periods

name: Foundries
description: Contract chip manufacturers - TSMC overwhelmingly, plus Samsung Foundry and Intel Foundry - that fabricate the world's leading-edge silicon.
whyItMatters: Leading-edge logic capacity is concentrated in one company on one island; foundry allocation decides which chip designers ship and which wait.
risks: Geopolitical concentration of leading-edge capacity in Taiwan
Enormous capex bets ahead of uncertain demand
Node-transition execution stumbles

name: Chip designers
description: Fabless and IP-led designers - NVIDIA, AMD, Qualcomm, Broadcom, Arm - that architect the chips foundries manufacture.
whyItMatters: Design is where most of the industry's margin and differentiation lives, and design wins decide where foundry and packaging capacity gets allocated.
risks: A missed product cycle cedes share for years
Customer concentration among hyperscalers
Export controls restrict top-end product sales

name: Semiconductor equipment
description: Wafer-fab equipment makers - ASML, Applied Materials, Lam Research, KLA, Tokyo Electron - whose tools define what chips can physically be made.
whyItMatters: ASML's EUV monopoly is the single most concentrated choke point in global technology; equipment shipments today are chip supply two years from now.
risks: Export controls cut off Chinese demand
Wafer-fab equipment spending is sharply cyclical
Their own sub-supplier base has single-source choke points

name: Semiconductor materials
description: Silicon wafers, photoresists, specialty gases and CMP slurries - Shin-Etsu, SUMCO, JSR, Linde - the consumables every wafer start burns through.
whyItMatters: Materials are low-glamour but irreplaceable: a photoresist or wafer shortage stops fabs as surely as a missing EUV tool, as Japan's export spat with Korea proved.
risks: Supply concentration in Japan invites policy shocks
Price pressure from fab customers with more leverage
Purity qualification barriers cut both ways for new entrants

name: Rare earth producers
description: Miners of rare earth elements outside China - MP Materials, Lynas, emerging projects - producing the feedstock for permanent magnets and defence systems.
whyItMatters: Rare earth magnets sit inside EVs, wind turbines, drones and missiles; Western producers are the only hedge against China's near-monopoly on supply.
risks: China sets prices and can flood the market
The processing gap outside China limits value capture
Permitting new mines takes the better part of a decade

name: Copper producers
description: The major copper miners - Freeport, BHP, Codelco, Southern Copper - supplying the metal that wires grids, data centres, EVs and motors.
whyItMatters: Copper is the common denominator of electrification and the AI power buildout; structural deficits are forecast as grades decline and demand compounds.
risks: Declining ore grades raise unit costs
Political and permitting risk in Chile, Peru and the DRC
New mines take over a decade from discovery to production

name: Processing and refining
description: The midstream that turns concentrate into usable metal and magnet alloy - a step China dominates with roughly 90 percent of rare earth refining and most gallium output.
whyItMatters: Mining ore means little without refining; the processing gap is the real Western vulnerability and the choke point China's export controls actually squeeze.
risks: China export controls weaponise the midstream
Environmental permitting slows Western capacity
Cost disadvantage versus incumbent Chinese refiners

name: Defence primes
description: The major contractors - Lockheed Martin, RTX, BAE, Rheinmetall, Northrop - integrating platforms and absorbing the bulk of rising Western defence budgets.
whyItMatters: Primes are the funded demand source of the theme: rearmament budgets flow through their order books into drones, counter-UAS and component suppliers below.
risks: Budget politics and continuing resolutions
Fixed-price development programs bleed margin
Their own supply chains gate delivery rates

name: Drones and autonomy
description: Unmanned systems and autonomy software - Anduril, AeroVironment, Kratos and a wave of startups - reshaping force structure after Ukraine proved cheap drones change wars.
whyItMatters: Attritable autonomous systems are the fastest-growing line in defence procurement, shifting spend from few exquisite platforms to many cheap ones.
risks: Slow procurement cycles lag battlefield demand
Dependence on Chinese components in small-drone supply chains
A crowded venture-funded field compresses pricing

name: Counter-UAS
description: Systems that detect and defeat hostile drones - radars, jammers, directed energy and interceptors from RTX, Rheinmetall, DroneShield and specialists.
whyItMatters: Every cheap attack drone creates demand for a defence; counter-UAS is the necessary mirror market to the drone boom and is moving from niche to program of record.
risks: Threats evolve faster than fielded countermeasures
Many competing approaches fragment program wins
Export restrictions limit addressable markets

name: Humanoid platforms
description: General-purpose humanoid robot programs - Tesla Optimus, Figure, Agility, Unitree - betting that one form factor can address labour shortages across industries.
whyItMatters: Humanoids are the demand thesis of the robotics theme: if they scale, they pull an automotive-sized supply chain of actuators, sensors and magnets into existence.
risks: Unit economics and reliability are still unproven
Hype runs far ahead of paid deployments
Chinese platforms compete aggressively on cost

name: Components and actuators
description: The precision guts of every robot - harmonic drives, servo motors, ball screws and reducers from Harmonic Drive Systems, Nidec, Regal Rexnord and peers.
whyItMatters: Each humanoid needs roughly 30-40 actuators; component capacity and rare earth magnet supply, not software, would gate any genuine production ramp.
risks: Rare earth magnet supply is a China-controlled input
Capacity additions lag if the humanoid ramp is real
Customer concentration in a few robot programs

name: Vision and sensors
description: Cameras, lidar, force-torque and tactile sensors plus the perception silicon - from Sony image sensors to specialist robotics sensing firms.
whyItMatters: Robots only act on what they perceive; sensor cost and capability set the floor on what tasks automation can reliably do outside a cage.
risks: Sensor hardware commoditises over time
Smartphone supply-chain giants enter at scale
Losing a design cycle locks vendors out for years

name: Security platforms
description: Broad security platforms - CrowdStrike, Palo Alto Networks, Fortinet, Microsoft Security - consolidating endpoint, network and cloud defence into single vendors.
whyItMatters: Security spend is among the least discretionary lines in enterprise IT, and AI raises both attack volume and the value of platform-scale telemetry.
risks: Platform consolidation wars compress smaller vendors
AI shifts the attack-defence balance unpredictably
A self-inflicted outage or breach destroys trust quickly

name: Identity and access
description: Identity providers and privileged access vendors - Okta, CyberArk, Microsoft Entra - controlling who and what can touch enterprise systems.
whyItMatters: Identity is the control plane of zero-trust security, and the coming wave of AI agents multiplies the machine identities that must be governed.
risks: Microsoft bundling pressures standalone vendors
A breach of an identity provider is existential
Agentic AI redraws the identity perimeter faster than products adapt

name: Quantum hardware
description: Quantum computer builders across modalities - IBM and Google superconducting, IonQ trapped ion, PsiQuantum photonic, Quantinuum - racing toward fault tolerance.
whyItMatters: Hardware progress is the entire thesis: error-corrected logical qubits are the milestone that would turn quantum from research spend into a real market.
risks: Commercial utility remains unproven at current scale
Pre-revenue names carry heavy dilution risk
The winning qubit modality is still undecided

name: Quantum enablers
description: The picks and shovels of quantum - cryogenics from Bluefors-class suppliers, control electronics, lasers, photonics and specialist test equipment.
whyItMatters: Every quantum lab and machine buys cryostats, lasers and control systems regardless of which modality wins, making enablers the lower-risk causal link in the theme.
risks: The addressable market is tiny today
Customer concentration in a handful of funded programs
A modality shift strands specialised tooling

name: Satellite components and subsystems
description: The merchant market for spacecraft power, propulsion and pointing hardware - solar cells and arrays from Rocket Lab's SolAero and Boeing's Spectrolab, Moog thrusters and actuation, star trackers, reaction wheels and precision timing from specialists like Frequency Electronics.
whyItMatters: Constellation-scale manufacturing multiplies demand for every subsystem, and a single sold-out component line - space solar cells especially - can gate an entire constellation's deployment schedule.
risks: Vertical integration by constellation owners shrinks the merchant market
Qualified solar cell and component capacity is concentrated in a handful of lines
Per-unit price deflation as satellite volumes scale

name: Critical materials and gases for space
description: The raw inputs at the bottom of the stack - aerospace-grade titanium and nickel superalloys from mills like ATI and Carpenter Technology, helium for tank pressurisation, xenon and krypton for electric propulsion, and germanium substrates for space solar cells.
whyItMatters: Every vehicle and satellite ultimately resolves to a narrow base of qualified mills and gas suppliers; sanctions on Russian titanium and Ukraine-driven noble-gas shortages showed how fast this layer can bind the chain above it.
risks: Commodity and gas price volatility swamps thin pure-play revenue pools
Russian titanium and Ukrainian noble-gas supply remain geopolitical fault lines
Aerospace qualification cycles keep new mills out for years

name: Generation equipment - turbines and generators
description: Gas turbines, steam turbines and generators from GE Vernova, Siemens Energy and Mitsubishi Power - the heavy machinery behind new dispatchable capacity. Delivery slots for large gas turbines are now reserved years in advance.
whyItMatters: Data-centre and electrification load is being met first with gas-fired capacity, making turbine delivery slots a sold-out, price-setting constraint.
risks: Order book overbuild if data-centre load disappoints
Capacity expansion normalises lead times later in the cycle
Policy swings between gas and renewables

name: Distribution equipment and grid edge
description: Distribution transformers, switchgear, meters, connectors and enclosures from Hubbell, Eaton, Schneider Electric and Itron that carry power the last mile to homes, factories and data centres.
whyItMatters: Distribution transformer shortages have become as acute as large power transformers, and every electrified end use multiplies the equipment count at the grid edge.
risks: New distribution transformer capacity relieves pricing
Housing and construction slowdowns cut baseline demand
Commodity input cost swings

name: Grid software and metering intelligence
description: The ADMS, DERMS and metering platforms - Itron, GE Vernova's GridOS, Schneider Electric and Oracle Utilities - that let utilities squeeze more throughput from existing wires and manage distributed resources.
whyItMatters: When new hardware takes years to arrive, software that unlocks capacity from the installed grid becomes the fastest deployable megawatt.
risks: Utility software sales cycles are slow
Competition from large industrial software incumbents
Cyber incidents could reshape procurement

name: Wire, cable and conductors
description: High- and medium-voltage cable, overhead conductor and conduit from Prysmian, Nexans, Southwire and Atkore - the copper and aluminium arteries of every grid project. HVDC and subsea cable capacity is booked years ahead.
whyItMatters: Cable plants and conductor capacity are a quieter bottleneck than transformers, but no transmission line gets energised without them.
risks: Metal price pass-through lags squeeze margins
New cable plant capacity arrives later this decade
Project delays push out deliveries

name: Electrical steel and transformer cores
description: Grain-oriented electrical steel (GOES) - the specialised core laminations inside every transformer - with Cleveland-Cliffs the only US producer and most non-Chinese supply from Japan, Korea and Europe.
whyItMatters: GOES supply is the raw-material chokepoint behind the transformer shortage; without more of it, transformer capacity expansions cannot deliver.
risks: Trade policy reshapes import availability
New GOES capacity is slow and capital intensive
Amorphous core substitution in some transformer classes

name: Copper and aluminium supply
description: The upstream metal producers - Freeport-McMoRan, Southern Copper, BHP, Alcoa - whose output feeds every conductor, transformer winding and busbar in the buildout.
whyItMatters: Grid expansion is among the most copper-intensive activities in the economy; long-dated mine supply decides whether the buildout's inputs stay affordable.
risks: Copper price cyclicality overwhelms the structural story
Mine development timelines stretch past a decade
Aluminium substitution for copper at the margin

name: Nuclear utilities and fleet operators
description: Operators of the existing reactor fleet - Constellation, Vistra, Talen, Duke, Dominion - signing long-dated hyperscaler power deals and restarting shuttered units like Three Mile Island Unit 1 and Palisades.
whyItMatters: The operating fleet is where nuclear demand meets revenue today: PPAs and restarts convert data-centre power hunger into contracted fuel and capacity demand for everything upstream.
risks: Regulatory pushback on co-located and behind-the-meter deals
Hedges and regulated tariffs cap upside from power prices
A single extended plant outage can dominate earnings

name: Reactor components, services and instrumentation
description: Makers of nuclear-qualified reactor systems, pumps, instrumentation and outage services - BWX Technologies, Curtiss-Wright, Mirion, GE Vernova's nuclear arm - serving the operating fleet, refurbishments and new builds.
whyItMatters: Every life extension, uprate, restart and SMR order flows through a small pool of certified manufacturers whose qualifications take years to earn and cannot be quickly replicated.
risks: New-build delays push order books to the right
Nuclear-qualified welders and engineers are themselves scarce
Long-cycle fixed-price contracts carry cost overrun risk

name: Uranium conversion
description: The UF6 conversion step between mining and enrichment, concentrated in a handful of Western sites - Cameco's Port Hope, ConverDyn's Metropolis plant and Orano's French facilities, with Westinghouse working to restart conversion at Springfields.
whyItMatters: Conversion is the thinnest link in the Western fuel cycle - prices rose severalfold after 2021 because conversion capacity, not mined uranium, set the binding constraint.
risks: Restarted Metropolis capacity can loosen the market over time
A single-site outage ripples through the whole fuel cycle
No listed pure play, so investable exposure is indirect

name: Uranium developers and restarts
description: Development-stage projects and restart pipelines - NexGen's Rook I, Denison's Wheeler River, and the US in-situ recovery wave led by UEC, enCore and Ur-Energy - that form the next tranche of supply.
whyItMatters: The gap between reactor demand and mine supply only closes if this pipeline delivers, and it is where permitting slippage, financing risk and dilution concentrate.
risks: Construction and permitting slippage is the norm, not the exception
Financing windows open and close with uranium sentiment
Many projects need incentive prices above the current term price

name: Physical uranium and royalties
description: Vehicles that hold pounds rather than mines - Sprott Physical Uranium Trust, Yellow Cake and Uranium Royalty Corp - absorbing spot supply and financing miners through royalties and streams.
whyItMatters: Physical trusts removed tens of millions of pounds from the spot market and now act as the marginal buyer that sets the visible price signal for the entire chain.
risks: Discounts to net asset value can persist for years
Trust buying stalls when units trade below NAV
Royalty value depends on mines actually reaching production

name: Mining inputs and wellfield services
description: The consumables and services beneath the miners - sulphuric acid for in-situ recovery, drilling contractors and wellfield construction - where shortages have already cut Kazatomprom's stated production plans.
whyItMatters: The raw upstream constraint is no longer just ore: Kazatomprom publicly blamed sulphuric acid shortages for production downgrades in 2024-2025, making acid and drilling capacity a genuine supply governor.
risks: Acid supply normalises as new plants commission
Service cost inflation squeezes miner margins
Few listed pure plays, so exposure is mostly indirect

name: Chip end demand
description: The device and system makers that consume finished chips - Apple, Dell, HPE, the hyperscalers and global automakers - whose product cycles set semiconductor volumes.
whyItMatters: Every wafer start ultimately clears through a phone, server, car or appliance, so end-market inventory and refresh cycles decide when the semiconductor cycle turns.
risks: Consumer electronics demand is mature and cyclical
Inventory corrections cascade down the whole chain
Tariffs on finished electronics reshape demand maps

name: EDA software and IP
description: The design-tool duopoly of Synopsys and Cadence plus architecture licensors like Arm - the software and IP without which no advanced chip can be designed.
whyItMatters: EDA access has become an export-control weapon: two US companies gate the design of essentially every leading-edge chip on earth.
risks: Export-control policy swings on China EDA access
AI-assisted design tools could reshape who captures value
Customer consolidation concentrates renewal risk

name: Power and analog semiconductors
description: Power, analog and mixed-signal chipmakers - Texas Instruments, Analog Devices, Infineon, onsemi, Monolithic Power - plus GaN and SiC specialists like Navitas serving AI data-centre power delivery and vehicles.
whyItMatters: AI racks moving toward 800-volt power architectures and electrifying vehicles both multiply power-semiconductor content, in a tier far less crowded than GPU designers.
risks: Analog inventory cycles produce long corrections
Chinese domestic substitution in commodity analog
SiC and GaN price competition erodes early margins

name: Packaging, assembly and test
description: The OSATs - Amkor, ASE, JCET - and the test ecosystem of Teradyne, Advantest and FormFactor that assemble, package and verify chips after wafer fabrication.
whyItMatters: Advanced packaging and known-good-die testing have become gating steps for AI silicon, and CHIPS-funded onshoring is rebuilding this tier in the US for the first time in decades.
risks: Thin OSAT margins versus foundries taking packaging in-house
Heavy geographic concentration in Taiwan and Southeast Asia
Utilisation swings amplify earnings cyclicality

name: Equipment subsystems and components
description: The sub-suppliers behind the tool makers - MKS Instruments, Advanced Energy, Ultra Clean, Ichor, VAT - providing RF power, vacuum, gas delivery and precision components inside ASML, Applied Materials and Lam Research tools.
whyItMatters: Every equipment order fans out into this quieter tier, where single-qualified components create choke points the headline equipment names depend on.
risks: Subsystem orders swing harder than OEM equipment revenue
Concentration on a handful of equipment OEM customers
Qualification lock-in cuts both ways when platforms change

name: Critical raw inputs
description: The rawest upstream inputs - ultra-pure polysilicon from Hemlock and Wacker, high-purity quartz from Spruce Pine, gallium, germanium, neon and helium - that every fab and wafer maker consumes.
whyItMatters: China's export controls on gallium and germanium showed this deepest tier can be weaponised, and single-site concentrations like Spruce Pine quartz have no quick substitutes.
risks: Chinese export controls on gallium and germanium
Single-site supply concentration for high-purity quartz
Opaque pricing in thin, specialised markets

name: Defence and electrification end demand
description: The end markets that consume critical minerals - defence primes like Lockheed Martin and RTX, EV makers like Tesla and GM, and wind and grid OEMs like GE Vernova - whose magnets, batteries and motors resolve to mined material.
whyItMatters: Procurement and stockpiling decisions at this tier set demand and the premium buyers will pay for non-Chinese supply, which is what makes the rest of the chain financeable.
risks: EV demand softness reduces mineral pull-through
Substitution engineering cuts rare earth content per unit
Defence budgets shift with political cycles

name: Permanent magnet manufacturing
description: Sintered NdFeB magnet plants outside China - MP Materials' Fort Worth facility, e-VAC's South Carolina plant, USA Rare Earth's Stillwater site - turning refined oxides and metal into finished magnets for defence and EV motors.
whyItMatters: Magnets are where refined rare earths become defence and EV components, and ex-China magnet capacity remains a small fraction of Western demand.
risks: Chinese export controls squeeze feedstock as well as competition
Ramp and yield execution at first-of-a-kind Western plants
Defence and auto qualification cycles are slow

name: Battery materials and conversion
description: Battery-grade lithium conversion, cathode and anode materials, and synthetic graphite - Albemarle's conversion plants, Novonix's Chattanooga anode facility, Tesla's Corpus Christi lithium refinery.
whyItMatters: Like rare earth separation, battery-grade conversion is a midstream step China dominates, and graphite export licensing made closing that gap an explicit Western policy priority.
risks: Chinese oversupply keeps conversion margins thin
Western cathode and anode plants face brutal cost curves against incumbents
Chemistry shifts like LFP and sodium-ion reshuffle input demand

name: Lithium producers
description: The miners of spodumene and brine - Albemarle, SQM, and emerging US supply led by Lithium Americas' Thacker Pass - feeding the battery chain's base metal.
whyItMatters: Lithium has no practical substitute in EV and storage batteries, and the post-2022 price crash curtailed exactly the supply the 2030s demand curve needs.
risks: Prices are set by marginal Chinese and African supply
Brine and clay projects carry novel process risk
Demand growth is hostage to EV adoption rates

name: Mining equipment and services
description: The trucks, shovels, drills and contractors every mine buildout must hire - Caterpillar and Komatsu fleets, Epiroc drilling systems, and the EPC and drilling firms that construct new operations.
whyItMatters: Long equipment lead times and scarce skilled contractors add years and capex to every new Western mine, making this tier a quiet tax on the whole buildout.
risks: Mining capex cycles swing orders violently
Exposure is diluted across all commodities, not just critical minerals
Fleet electrification raises the R&D burden

name: Exploration and pre-production development
description: Pre-revenue developers and explorers holding the West's undeveloped deposits - Perpetua's Stibnite antimony-gold project, NioCorp's Elk Creek, Ramaco's Brook Mine rare earth seams - plus the grassroots drill plays behind them.
whyItMatters: This is the rawest upstream bottleneck: with 10-15 years from discovery to production, today's permitting and financing queue IS the 2030s Western supply curve.
risks: Most projects never secure construction financing
Permitting timelines are measured in decades, not years
Equity dilution is the default funding model

name: Defence software and battle management
description: Software-defined command, control and targeting layers - Palantir's Maven and TITAN work, Anduril's Lattice - that fuse sensor data and task autonomous systems across a battlefield.
whyItMatters: Software is where the attritable-mass thesis earns technology margins: whoever owns the C2 layer directs the drones, sensors and effectors below it.
risks: Primes and government-owned software compete for the same layer
Program awards are politically contested and frequently protested
Classified work limits outside visibility into performance

name: Munitions and solid rocket motors
description: Missiles, artillery shells, interceptors and the solid rocket motors and energetics beneath them - Lockheed, RTX, Northrop and L3Harris Aerojet lines running at replenishment rates after Ukraine drained Western stockpiles.
whyItMatters: Every rearmament budget flows into a munitions industrial base where motor and energetics capacity, not funding, is the limiter on delivery rates.
risks: Energetic materials and precursor chemicals are single-sourced
New facilities take years to build and qualify
A broad de-escalation would slow replenishment urgency

name: Defence electronics and sensors
description: Radars, electro-optics, electronic warfare, seekers and rugged mission computing - Leonardo DRS, Elbit, Mercury Systems and L3Harris units embedded in nearly every platform and munition.
whyItMatters: Sensor and EW content per platform keeps rising - drones, counter-UAS and precision munitions are all guided by this layer's chips and apertures.
risks: Component obsolescence and long qualification cycles
Consolidated prime customers squeeze suppliers on price
Export controls on GaN and RF parts limit addressable markets

name: Small-drone components
description: Motors, flight controllers, gimbals, radios and batteries for small UAS - a supply chain dominated by China's DJI ecosystem that NDAA rules now force Western vendors like Unusual Machines to rebuild onshore.
whyItMatters: Every Western small-drone program is gated by non-Chinese component supply - the theme's most explicit reshoring bottleneck sits in this tier.
risks: Chinese components remain drastically cheaper without policy mandates
Sub-scale Western vendors depend on procurement protection
Standards churn across drone programs fragments volumes

name: Castings, forgings and aerostructures
description: Precision castings, forgings and specialty-alloy structures from Howmet, Carpenter Technology, ATI and Ducommun that become airframes, engine parts and missile bodies.
whyItMatters: Forging and casting throughput is the physical limit under every missile and airframe ramp - lead times in this tier set delivery rates above it.
risks: Capacity added for the ramp becomes overhang in a downturn
Skilled foundry and forge labour is scarce
Alloy input price swings squeeze fixed-price contracts

name: Defence critical materials
description: The raw inputs the whole chain resolves to - rare earth magnets for drone motors and guidance fins, titanium sponge, gallium for radar semiconductors and energetic precursors - much of it processed in China.
whyItMatters: China's export controls on gallium, germanium and rare earths target this tier directly, making it the deepest and most policy-sensitive link in the defence supply chain.
risks: Chinese export controls can halt shipments abruptly
Western substitution capacity is years from scale
Stockpiling policy shifts distort demand signals

name: Warehouse and industrial automation
description: Deployed automation that already earns revenue - Symbotic case-handling systems, Amazon Robotics fleets, and industrial arms and cells from FANUC, ABB, Yaskawa and Rockwell-integrated lines.
whyItMatters: This is where robotics economics are already proven; installed-base growth here funds and de-risks the component supply chain the humanoid thesis will eventually need.
risks: Warehouse capex tracks the e-commerce cycle
Heavy customer concentration in a few retail giants
Chinese integrators compress system pricing

name: Surgical and medical robotics
description: Robotic surgery platforms with razor-and-blade economics - Intuitive Surgical's da Vinci installed base, Stryker Mako, Medtronic Hugo and Procept BioRobotics' Aquabeam.
whyItMatters: Surgical robotics proves robots can command premium pricing when they earn recurring instrument revenue per procedure - the business model every other robot category wants.
risks: Regulatory approval cycles are long and binary
Hospital capex sensitivity delays system placements
Incumbent moats leave little room for new entrants

name: Robot foundation models and simulation
description: The software brains and training pipelines - NVIDIA Isaac and GR00T, Google DeepMind robotics models, Physical Intelligence, and the sim-to-real toolchains that generate manipulation training data.
whyItMatters: Manipulation training data and transferable robot policies are the theme's stated binding constraint - whoever cracks generalisation sets the humanoid timeline.
risks: Open-source robot models compress software value
The sim-to-real gap keeps resisting shortcuts
Most of the strongest teams are private

name: Robot compute and motion-control silicon
description: Edge AI computers and control chips inside every robot - NVIDIA Jetson Thor, Qualcomm robotics platforms, Ambarella vision SoCs, and the analog motion-control and power silicon from TI, ADI and STMicroelectronics.
whyItMatters: Every actuator and camera terminates in silicon; robot bill-of-materials shifts toward compute as autonomy rises, mirroring the electronics ramp inside cars.
risks: Industrial and auto analog demand is deeply cyclical
Chinese MCU substitution at the commodity end
One platform vendor could capture the whole compute layer

name: Robot batteries and power systems
description: High energy-density cells, packs and power electronics for mobile robots and humanoids - drawing on the same lithium-ion supply chain as EVs, dominated by CATL, LG Energy Solution and Panasonic, with silicon-anode specialists like Amprius pushing density.
whyItMatters: Battery life is a named binding constraint on humanoids - runtime per charge decides whether a robot does a full shift of work or none.
risks: EV demand sets cell pricing, not robotics
Energy density improves far slower than compute
China dominates cell manufacturing capacity

name: Rare earth magnets and motor materials
description: Sintered NdFeB permanent magnets and the mined rare earths behind them - MP Materials, Lynas and USA Rare Earth building ex-China supply against a market where China controls most refining and magnet output.
whyItMatters: Every servo motor in every actuator needs NdFeB magnets; China's export controls on rare earths make this the deepest single point of failure in the robotics chain.
risks: China export controls and price influence
Ex-China processing capacity is years away at scale
Commodity price swings swamp equity fundamentals

name: Government cyber and mission services
description: Federal cyber operations, compliance automation and mission IT delivered by Leidos, Booz Allen Hamilton, CACI and Telos into the DoD, intelligence community and civilian agencies.
whyItMatters: Government is the stickiest end demand in security - multi-year contract vehicles and rising nation-state threat activity keep budgets growing through commercial IT cycles.
risks: Continuing-resolution funding gaps delay awards
Cost-plus contracting structurally caps margins
Efficiency-driven cuts to contractor spend

name: Network, edge and cloud security
description: Cloud-delivered network defence and secure access service edge - Zscaler, Cloudflare, Fortinet, Netskope - replacing appliance perimeters as traffic moves to cloud and remote work.
whyItMatters: The enterprise perimeter is being rebuilt in the cloud, and whoever carries the traffic controls the inspection point for everything else in the stack.
risks: Hardware-to-SaaS transition cannibalises firewall vendors
Hyperscalers bundle native network security
Price competition intensifies as SASE matures

name: Security operations, SIEM and AI SOC
description: The detection-and-response layer - Splunk under Cisco, Microsoft Sentinel, CrowdStrike and SentinelOne AI SIEM, Rapid7 - where security telemetry is aggregated and increasingly triaged by AI agents.
whyItMatters: The security analyst shortage makes the SOC the natural first home for AI agents, and whoever owns the telemetry owns the data advantage for training them.
risks: Ingest-based pricing breaks as telemetry volumes explode
AI SOC agents deflate analyst- and seat-based pricing
Platform vendors absorb standalone SIEM

name: Data security, encryption and post-quantum migration
description: Data resilience, encryption and key management - Rubrik, Varonis, Commvault, Thales - plus the multi-year migration of certificates, HSMs and protocols to the NIST post-quantum standards finalised in 2024.
whyItMatters: Ransomware turned backup into a security product, and the decade-long post-quantum re-encryption of global infrastructure is one of the few genuinely new spend cycles in a mature theme.
risks: Post-quantum migration timelines keep slipping right
Backup incumbents and hyperscalers bundle data security
Crypto-agility standards commoditise point vendors

name: Security hardware and silicon
description: The physical trust anchors - Fortinet's custom SPU ASICs, hardware security modules from Thales and Utimaco, NXP and Infineon secure elements, and NVIDIA BlueField DPUs that offload security processing.
whyItMatters: Every zero-trust architecture ultimately roots in tamper-resistant silicon, and line-rate inspection of AI-era traffic increasingly requires dedicated hardware rather than general-purpose CPUs.
risks: Cloud delivery shifts value from appliances to software
Long certification cycles slow product refreshes
Secure-element supply concentrated in a few vendors

name: Trusted foundry and secure chip supply
description: Accredited onshore fabrication of defence and security-critical chips - GlobalFoundries' DMEA-accredited Trusted Foundry fabs in Vermont and New York, plus Intel's secure-enclave programs for the DoD.
whyItMatters: Security guarantees are only as strong as the supply chain that made the silicon, which makes accredited onshore fabs the raw upstream bottleneck of the entire trust stack.
risks: Mature-node economics depend on subsidy support
Accreditation limits the supplier pool to a handful of fabs
Defence chip demand is lumpy against commercial cycles

name: Quantum software and post-quantum cryptography
description: Algorithm developers, error-correction software and the post-quantum cryptography migration - IBM's Qiskit ecosystem, Quantinuum, SandboxAQ, SEALSQ and Arqit - where NIST-standardised PQC gives the theme revenue before the hardware matures.
whyItMatters: PQC migration is mandated by published NIST standards and paid for from existing enterprise security budgets, making it the nearest-term real revenue anywhere in the theme.
risks: PQC spend flows mostly to incumbent security vendors
Quantum software has little moat without hardware advantage
Migration timelines slip as enterprises defer spend

name: Quantum networking and sensing
description: Quantum key distribution, quantum-safe networks, atomic clocks and quantum sensors - IonQ's networking acquisitions, Toshiba's QKD systems and defence sensing programs - productising quantum physics ahead of full computers.
whyItMatters: Networking and sensing monetise quantum effects years before fault-tolerant computing arrives, anchored by government and defence buyers with real budgets.
risks: Government-dominated demand is lumpy and political
Classical alternatives undercut QKD economics
Quantum network standards remain immature

name: Photonics, lasers and detectors
description: Precision lasers, modulators, single-photon detectors and photonic integrated circuits - from Coherent, Hamamatsu, Thorlabs and Quantum Computing Inc's lithium niobate foundry - consumed by trapped-ion, neutral-atom and photonic machines.
whyItMatters: Three of the four leading qubit modalities are built from photonics, so laser and detector supply is a common input regardless of which platform wins.
risks: Quantum is a tiny share of overall photonics demand
Specialised components carry single-source supply risk
A superconducting-modality win reduces photonics content

name: Quantum chip fabrication
description: Specialised foundry services for superconducting and photonic quantum chips - GlobalFoundries manufacturing PsiQuantum's photonic wafers, SkyWater fabricating superconducting devices for D-Wave, and Rigetti's own in-house fab.
whyItMatters: Qubit chips need semiconductor-grade process control years before volumes justify it, so a handful of qualified fab lines gate every hardware roadmap.
risks: Volumes are far too small for normal foundry economics
Process knowledge concentrated in a few lines
A modality shift strands tooling investment

name: Superconducting materials and wire
description: Niobium, niobium-titanium wire and tantalum films that superconducting qubits, resonators and cryostat wiring are made from - niobium supply dominated by Brazil's CBMM, with wire specialists such as Bruker's superconductor unit and Luvata.
whyItMatters: Superconducting qubits and the wiring and magnets around them resolve to a thin industrial base of niobium and tantalum products with very few qualified sources.
risks: Niobium supply concentrated in a single Brazilian producer
Quantum volumes are negligible for materials suppliers
Formulation shifts change which materials matter

name: Helium and isotopes
description: Liquid helium, scarce helium-3 for dilution refrigerators and isotopically enriched silicon-28 - bulk helium supplied by industrial gas majors like Linde and Air Products, while helium-3 is largely a byproduct of government tritium stockpiles.
whyItMatters: Every superconducting machine sits inside a dilution refrigerator that cannot run without helium isotopes, the rawest and least substitutable input in the entire chain.
risks: Helium-3 supply is a government byproduct with no market elasticity
Helium prices spike on plant outages and export disruptions
Closed-loop recycling reduces per-machine demand over time
